newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bombs kill one, wound 30 in western Algeria-paper.
newsitem.headline: Bombs kill one, wound 30 in western Algeria-paper.

text.p: Two bombs exploded almost simultaneously in two cafes in the western Algerian town of Tlemcen, killing one person and wounding 30, an Algerian newspaper said on Sunday.
The home-made bombs ripped through the cafes in central Tlemcen at about 10.30 a.m. (0930 GMT) on Saturday destroying the two coffee shops, El Watan newspaper said.
The first explosion at Le Palmier cafe in Bab Zir district killed a man aged about 50. The second blast hit another cafe near a prison in the centre of Tlemcen, said El Watan.
A total of 30 people were wounded, it said.
A huge blast rocked Tlemcen on May 24, the first day of campaigning for Algeria's June 5 general election, killing several people, according to Algerian papers.
El Watan said five attacks occured in Tlemcen in the past two months in addition to other attacks along a main road linking the city to neighbouring Nedroma town.
The reported bombs were the latest in a series of blasts marking the bloody trail of Algeria's five and half years of violence pitting Moslem guerrillas against government forces.

At least 21 people were killed last week when a bomb ripped through an Algiers market crowded with women shoppers and children. The authorities blame Moslem rebels for the bombings and other attacks targeting ordinary civilians.

More than 350 people have been killed in massacres of villagers in remote hamlets and in bomb attacks, mainly in Algiers, since the June election in which Algerians hoped would help end the conflict in their country.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead.

Last week, the authorities, apparently trying to broaden a consensus against radical Islamists, set free FIS chief Abassi Madani from prison, halfway through his 12-year sentence imposed in 1992 by a military court for threatening state security.

His release on parole came one week after FIS leader Abdelkader Hachani walked free from jail after he was sentenced to five years' imprisonment, a term covered by his preventive detention pending trial. The state prosecutor had asked for a sentence of 10 years.
